facts.text: Equalization is funded from federal general revenues. Provincial governments do not pay equalization to each other. Fiscal capacity and federal transfers are separate from pipeline tolls and shipment value.
Canada has no general provincial-border tariffs. Regulatory barriers, carrier tolls, royalties and applicable government fees are distinct.

The Bank of Canada distinguishes oil-price increases caused by supply disruptions from increases driven by stronger global demand. Producer income can rise while households and energy-using businesses face higher costs. Shock origin, persistence, ownership and exchange rates affect the net result.

Haisla Nation describes majority ownership and construction of the Cedar LNG project in its dated project update. Coastal First Nations state opposition to northern oil tanker traffic. These are named organizations discussing different projects and places. Neither position represents all Indigenous peoples, and a dated construction update does not establish current operating status.
Unifor argues for investment, maintenance, safe infrastructure and stable employment. Its statement is evidence of the union position, not an independently measured jobs forecast.

CAPP emphasizes investment, market access and petroleum economic contribution. It represents producer interests. Its claimed contributions require consistent direct, indirect and induced accounting before comparison with official GDP.

ECCC inventories measure territorial emissions. Lifecycle emissions, emissions intensity and total emissions answer different questions. Lower lifecycle emissions than coal do not establish that a particular LNG project displaces coal.
Pembina Institute questions LNG expansion through conditional climate, demand and market-risk analysis. Treat this as attributed stakeholder research, not observed future project returns.
IESO planning separates annual electricity demand from capacity and system adequacy. Planning scenarios are not realized demand or all-in retail bills.

Statistics Canada measures household energy burden under a specified census definition. Provincial GDP does not describe how costs and incomes are distributed within a province. The census analysis is historical, not a current household bill estimate.
